claims.text: The alloy has an equimolar W-Ta-Ti-V-Zr composition.
Multicomponent solutes segregate to grain boundaries in WTaTiVZr during thermomechanical processing.
Grain-boundary solute segregation lowers the grain-boundary energy of WTaTiVZr.
Grain-boundary solute segregation increases grain-boundary cohesion in WTaTiVZr.
Enhanced grain-boundary cohesion delays intergranular crack initiation.
Enhanced grain-boundary cohesion slows intergranular crack propagation.
Delayed intergranular cracking enables greater plastic deformation before failure.
Pure tungsten lacks the proposed multicomponent-solute grain-boundary cohesion benefit.
At 800–1200 °C, WTaTiVZr will exhibit greater plastic strain at failure than commercially pure tungsten with comparable grain size and processing history.
At 800–1200 °C, WTaTiVZr will exhibit higher fracture toughness than commercially pure tungsten with comparable grain size and processing history.
WTaTiVZr will show later crack initiation than pure tungsten under the specified high-temperature and irradiation conditions.
WTaTiVZr will show slower crack propagation than pure tungsten under the specified high-temperature and irradiation conditions.
WTaTiVZr will resist intergranular failure better than pure tungsten under the specified high-temperature and irradiation conditions.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply only when grain size and processing history are controlled and secondary phases, impurities, and processing inhomogeneities do not dominate.
The quantitative contribution of grain-boundary cohesion relative to matrix strengthening is uncertain.
Irradiation-induced microstructural changes may alter the proposed segregation-cohesion mechanism.
